statement: One move takes a point, reflects it across the line $y = x$, and then reflects the result across the $x$-axis. Ravi starts with the point $(5, 2)$ and makes this move $2027$ times in a row. Where does the point end up?

choices.misconception: I thought the point comes back to the start after every two moves, so an odd number of moves would leave it where one move does.
I found that the point repeats every four moves, but I counted the starting point as move $1$, so I landed one step too early in the cycle.
I thought each reflection across the $x$-axis just undoes the one before, so only the $2027$ reflections across $y = x$ matter, and an odd number of them sends $(5, 2)$ to $(2, 5)$.
I thought one move was the same as a single reflection across the line $y = -x$, so an odd number of moves would send $(5, 2)$ to $(-2, -5)$.

hints: Make the move a few times by hand and watch what happens to the coordinates.

Reflecting across $y = x$ swaps the coordinates, and reflecting across the $x$-axis changes the sign of the second one. So one move sends $(x, y)$ to $(y, -x)$. Keep going until you are back at $(5, 2)$.
The points go $(5, 2) \to (2, -5) \to (-5, -2) \to (-2, 5) \to (5, 2)$, a cycle of $4$ moves. Find the remainder when $2027$ is divided by $4$.

solutions.reliable: Reflecting $(x, y)$ across $y = x$ gives $(y, x)$, and then reflecting across the $x$-axis gives $(y, -x)$. So one move sends $(x, y)$ to $(y, -x)$. Starting from $(5, 2)$: after $1$ move $(2, -5)$, after $2$ moves $(-5, -2)$, after $3$ moves $(-2, 5)$, and after $4$ moves $(5, 2)$ again. The positions repeat every $4$ moves. Since $2027 = 4 \cdot 506 + 3$, the point ends where it is after $3$ moves, at $(-2, 5)$.
solutions.elegant: Two reflections across lines through the origin that meet at a $45^\circ$ angle combine into a rotation of $90^\circ$ about the origin. Here one move sends $(5, 2)$ to $(2, -5)$, a quarter turn clockwise. Then $2027$ quarter turns clockwise is $506$ full turns plus $3$ quarter turns clockwise, which is the same as one quarter turn counterclockwise. That sends $(5, 2)$ to $(-2, 5)$.
